source.title: Stress Testing Unlearning Algorithms
source.authors: Noam Diamant; Ethan Fetaya; Neta Glazer

page_placements.theme: Off-target effects on retained knowledge near the target (ripple, knowledge holes, over-generalization) that general benchmarks miss

record.tranche_reason: The study tests recovery after unlearning with in-context examples and jailbreak attacks. Its results qualify the claim: recovery depends on the unlearning method and attack, and it reports cases where the attacks leave accuracy near chance as well as cases with substantial increases.
record.gate_note: The study reports target accuracy, MMLU accuracy, in-context QA results, and three jailbreak results for multiple model, method, and domain combinations. Rows below include target and MMLU results and the GCG attack results. The text also discusses ICL, DIA, Crescendo, and the combined Max-JB metric; their results are not included as rows because of the 60-row limit. Cited results from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study applies existing unlearning methods (RMU, ELM, NPO, simNPO, OrthoGrad) to Llama-3-8B and Zephyr-7B on WMDP bio/cyber. It then attacks them with prompt-only extraction: enhanced GCG prefixes, DIA, Crescendo and in-context QA or paragraphs, scoring target accuracy. It argues that many methods suppress rather than erase. These are direct results on versions A and E. It is not one of the original sources.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that target accuracy alone fails to distinguish or rank methods (RMU and simNPO look alike but differ greatly under Max-JB). They find many methods suppress rather than erase, shown mainly by white-box GCG, while black-box and in-context attacks largely fail except on ELM. They also find MMLU/MMLUS miss severe collateral damage on near-distribution Boundary questions.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates several existing unlearning methods on WMDP biology and cybersecurity subsets, then adds ICL and jailbreak robustness evaluations; it is not a reproduction of one original method.
record.method_sensitivity: Recovery varies by unlearning method, model, domain, and attack. The authors report that enhanced GCG usually outperforms DIA and Crescendo, with exceptions; ICL recovery is especially notable for ELM in Biology. GCG uses attacked layers 5, 6, and 7.

fits_no_version.finding: Unlearning sharply degrades benign near-distribution 'Boundary' questions while MMLU/MMLUS look stable, e.g. Zephyr RMU bio Boundary 0.98→0.47 with MMLU ~1 pt drop (Tables 1-2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearning causes collateral damage to safe, conceptually adjacent knowledge that general retain benchmarks miss.

record.problems: No comparison to a model that never learned the targeted knowledge, limiting the claim that recovery exceeds what such a model can do. Only two model families are tested. The primary extraction measure is four-choice WMDP accuracy. The authors note that the Boundary dataset has 100 questions per domain and that biology questions were not human-validated. The text reports no uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: The 60-row limit is reached. Omitted separately reported results include MMLUS and Boundary scores in Tables 1-2; in-context QA accuracy in Tables 3-4; DIA and Crescendo scores in Tables 5-6; Max-JB scores in Tables 1-2; and paragraph-context and Wikipedia-context results in Figures 3-8. The GCG rows were retained as the attack-result subset, alongside Target and MMLU rows needed for version A.

untested.parts: No never-trained or retrained-from-scratch reference. General ability is measured only by MMLU (plus the MMLUS subset), not broader capabilities.
No fine-tuning or relearning attack of any kind.
No activation-direction ablation or internal analysis of suppression versus deletion.
Rephrasing and other-language prompts were not tested. PAIR was tried but excluded because its prefixes leaked answers.
No new method claimed robust to these attacks is proposed or tested.

missing.what: In-context few-shot QA recovery: mostly flat near chance, except ELM. Zephyr ELM bio rises 0.2663→0.5577 with MMLUS-QA context and 0.4705 with Boundary-QA context; Llama ELM bio rises 0.3323→0.3912. Bears on E (in-context information) but declared omitted.

Black-box jailbreaks: DIA and Crescendo mostly fail (≈0.25). Exceptions are Zephyr ELM bio (Crescendo 0.5405, DIA 0.4580) and Zephyr RMU cyber (DIA 0.3181 > GCG 0.3100). Declared omitted, but needed for the E verdict on black-box prompting.

record.verdict_notes: States for GCG rows (r41-r60) are scored against E (recovery occurs); for A, the same recovery counts against the version. Max-JB values in Tables 1-2 equal the max over GCG/DIA/Crescendo in Tables 5-6, so they are not separate results. Zephyr RMU, ELM, NPO and simNPO use authors' released checkpoints; Llama variants were tuned by this study. MMLU values are identical across the bio and cyber tables for shared checkpoints, despite captions saying 'MMLU biology/cybersecurity'. No uncertainty is reported, and GCG was optimized on questions the base gets right and the unlearned model gets wrong.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not compare against a model that never learned the targeted knowledge, so it cannot establish whether attack results exceed that reference. General ability is measured with MMLU, not across all capabilities.
No fine-tuning or relearning on unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten facts is tested.
No activation-direction ablation or internal-edit recovery test is conducted.

The study tests GCG and other jailbreaks, and in-context examples. It does not test prompt rephrasing, other languages, or jailbreaks beyond the methods described. ICL, DIA, Crescendo, and Max-JB results were tested but not extracted into rows because of the row limit.
No newer counter-method is tested for resistance to the attacks.
